But what actually made me come in today is that... well, for the past year or so, I just cannot stay on track. 

It's like the absolute smallest thing will happen and I'm totally derailed. Like, my phone will just give a tiny little buzz on the desk—not even a ring, just a quick vibration—and boom, I've dropped whatever important thing I'm doing to look at it. Or, you know, I have this office with the big glass walls, which I thought was a great leadership move for transparency, but if somebody just walks past my door to go to the breakroom, I'm suddenly watching them and wondering what they're up to instead of looking at my screen. 

And it’s not even just stuff I can see or hear in the office! I’ll be right in the middle of something critical, and then I’ll have a totally random thought—like about my in-laws, because they're coming to visit soon and they always have something to say about the guest room—and before I can even stop it, it just pulls me completely off what I’m doing. Next thing I know, twenty minutes have gone by and I'm looking at mattress reviews online instead of finalizing my contracts. It just pulls me right away before I can even catch myself doing it, and it's been driving me absolutely crazy for a solid year now.

turns.doctor_question: Before age 12, did you also have trouble staying focused on schoolwork or listening to the teacher, or was it mainly the hyperactive and impulsive behavior?

Yeah, so, like I was just saying a second ago, it really was strictly the hyperactive and impulsive stuff. I had absolutely zero trouble listening to the teachers or focusing on the actual schoolwork. In fact, it was almost the exact opposite. And of course, that's when the trouble would start, because I couldn't just sit there quietly. 

I remember specifically in fourth grade, I had this teacher, Mrs. Gable. Strict older woman, always wore this incredibly strong floral perfume you could smell from down the hall. She was absolutely convinced I never listened to a word she said because I was never looking at her. One time, she was doing this whole long lesson on fractions on the overhead projector, and I was literally under my desk. I had found a loose screw on the metal leg of the chair and I was trying to tighten it with a paperclip. She stopped the whole class, completely silent, and called my name, obviously trying to catch me not paying attention to make an example out of me. She asked me what the common denominator was for whatever she had just put on the board. And without even pulling my head out from under the desk, I just rattled off the exact right answer. 

I didn't have trouble focusing on the work. Honestly, the work was usually just way too slow. I didn't need them to repeat things three times for me to get it. So while they were droning on for the rest of the class, my brain was already ten steps ahead. I think my body was just doing its own thing—tapping, moving, talking, taking apart my pens—because I was under-stimulated by the pace, not because I couldn't focus. I absorbed everything. My brain just didn't require me to be glued to a chair, facing forward with my hands folded, to process the information, you know? So no, staying focused on the lessons was never the problem back then. It was one hundred percent just the fact that I couldn't contain my physical energy while they were teaching.

And it’s the exact same thing with those planning documents. I'll start reading, get through the first page feeling great, and then suddenly realize my eyes are just moving over the paper but absolutely zero information is actually going into my brain.
